summary: Floor control manages joint or exclusive access to shared resources in multiparty conferences, complementing session setup, conference policy, and media control. This document defines requirements for a floor control protocol in the context of an existing conferencing framework. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: In a meeting, only one person talks at a time. This lists what a system needs to decide who holds the talking stick.

questions: how does floor control work in conferences
subtitle: Framework for managing who speaks in group conferences

tldr.problem: In multiparty conferences, multiple participants want to speak simultaneously, so the system needs rules to manage exclusive or shared access to shared resources like the right to speak.
tldr.mechanism: A floor control protocol manages requests from participants, decisions by a floor chair (moderator), and notifications to all conference members about who holds the floor.
tldr.outcome: Participants can safely request, hold, or release exclusive control over conference resources without interrupting each other or misusing media streams.

facts.label: Main entities
facts.value: Floor control server, floor chair, participants

facts.label: Message types
facts.value: Floor requests, grants, denials, revocations, notifications

today: RFC 4376 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted or updated. It establishes the requirements framework that floor control protocol implementations must follow to work in IETF conferencing contexts.

sections.title: Why Floor Control Matters
sections.content:
Conferences bring many people together to collaborate, and they need to share limited resources. A conference participant might want to speak (audio), control a video feed, use a shared whiteboard, or click a mouse pointer in a shared application. Without rules, chaos erupts: everyone tries to speak at once, or one person monopolizes the audio. Floor control is the mechanism that manages exclusive or shared temporary access to these resources.

An RFC defines the floor as a permission to access or manipulate a specific shared resource or set of resources temporarily. Floor control is optional; some applications do not need it. But for applications that do, the protocol must work with other conferencing functions like session setup, policy control, and media handling.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of people in a meeting want to use the same things, but they can't all use them at once. Floor control decides who gets to use what and when.

sections.title: The Architecture: Three Players
sections.content:
The RFC describes a three-player model. A floor control server is a central point that keeps track of all the floors, who requested them, who holds them, and who the floor chairs are. Floor chairs (moderators) make decisions: they grant, deny, or revoke access to the floor, or they automate the decision through policy. Regular conference participants request floors, receive notifications about who has them, and operate within the rules. All messages flow through the server as a single point of control.

The floor chair does not have to be a participant. The conference owner (who may or may not be in the conference) sets up the floors, appoints the chairs, and defines the floor policy. The floor control server is often co-located with the conference focus or policy server, but the RFC does not mandate this.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a moderator (floor chair) who decides who gets the talking stick, a central person (server) who keeps track and passes messages, and everyone else who wants to talk.

sections.title: Participant and Chair Operations
sections.content:
Participants must be able to request a floor, provide optional information about why they want it (e.g., the topic of a question), and cancel or modify a request. They must receive clear notifications when their request is granted, denied, or pending. If they hold the floor, they must be able to release it at any time. The protocol must also support third-party floor control: one participant can request or release a floor on behalf of another (if authorized to do so).

Floor chairs receive notifications about new floor requests and can grant, deny, or revoke floors from participants. They can manipulate the queue of pending requests: reorder them, clear them, or pass the floor to someone else. The chairs can hide the identity of a requesting participant (for anonymous voting or anonymous questions) and hide their own identity from participants if desired. A newly assigned chair must be able to ask the server about the current queue of pending requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Participants ask for the floor and get told yes, no, or wait. The moderator decides who gets it, and can handle anonymous requests.

sections.title: Policy Control and Security
sections.content:
Floor control does not define policy; instead, the conference policy defines the rules. The policy must specify whether floor control is in use, what algorithm grants the floor (moderator-controlled, first-come-first-served, random, etc.), how many participants can hold a floor at once, which media are floor-controlled, and whether the floor chair can be replaced. The floor control protocol must be reliable (deliver or report errors) and authenticate all parties. Messages must be integrity-protected and optionally encrypted to prevent attackers from spoofing a participant, injecting false floor grants, or eavesdropping on who is present and how active they are.

The RFC discusses threats: an attacker could impersonate a participant and block them from speaking, inject false notifications, or intercept messages between the chair and server to disrupt the conference. Bandwidth must be managed efficiently, especially in mobile environments where bandwidth is limited. The protocol should allow both expressive messages (with detailed reasons) and minimal messages (just the bare request).
sections.plainLanguage: The system must keep attackers from pretending to be someone else, muting people unfairly, or listening in on who is in the meeting. It should also work on slow connections.

sections.title: Fitting into the Conferencing Framework
sections.content:
The RFC uses concepts from the IETF Conferencing Framework. The floor control server, floor chair, and participants can map to the framework's focus, policy server, and conference members, but the RFC itself makes no strict assumptions. A floor control protocol could be implemented within SIP, CPCP (Conference Policy Control Protocol), or any other signaling protocol.

Conferences can be hierarchical: a subconference can be represented as a single participant in a parent conference. The floor control protocol operates at the signaling level, but actual enforcement (muting the audio of a participant who does not hold the floor, blocking their video) is recommended but outside the scope of this requirements document. That job belongs to media servers and conference policy, which are controlled separately.
sections.plainLanguage: Floor control is just one piece of a bigger conference system. Other parts handle creating the conference, setting rules, and blocking audio or video if needed.

sections.title: Practical Use Cases
sections.content: In a large town hall meeting, the moderator controls a single audio floor and several video floors for breakout sessions. Participants request the audio floor to ask questions, and the chair grants or denies based on a queue or policy. In a collaborative whiteboard session, multiple participants might hold the drawing floor simultaneously. In an academic seminar, students submit anonymous questions, and the instructor decides which ones to discuss. In all cases, floor control provides the protocol framework for these decisions and notifications, while conference policy and media control handle the actual rules and enforcement.
sections.plainLanguage: A moderator can let one person speak, many people draw together, or let people ask questions secretly. Floor control makes it all work.
